title: A Korean School Sport
bigQuestion: How did South Korea build taekwondo into a national sport and bring it to the Olympics?

story.title: A Booklet for Every School
story.kicker: In the 1960s, a young national sport group in Seoul set out to give many halls one name and one plan.
paragraphs: Picture Seoul in the 1960s. The Korean War ended in 1953, and the city is still rebuilding. Busy streets hold small training halls. Each hall, called a kwan, has its own founder, its own name and its own habits.
Leaders from these halls have agreed to work together in one national association. Their art has a new name, taekwondo. The name was chosen in 1955. Not every teacher uses it yet.

The association wants the same art taught in the same way in schools and army camps. Printed rule books and rank lists help with that. A student in Busan and a student in Seoul could now test for the same rank.

Some teachers worry that their hall's own ways will be lost. Others hope one national art will make Korea proud after years of colonial rule and war. Their choices shaped a sport now practiced in more than 200 countries.
story.think: What might a teacher gain, and what might a teacher lose, when many halls join one national group?

lessons.title: Ssireum and Taekkyeon
lessons.mainIdea: Korea had older movement games, like ssireum wrestling and taekkyeon, long before taekwondo was named.
reading: Korean wrestling is called *ssireum*. People held matches at village festivals and holidays for centuries. A winner often took home a bull as a prize. In 2018, North Korea and South Korea asked UNESCO together to list ssireum as world heritage. It was the first joint listing by the two Koreas.

An old Korean movement game is called *taekkyeon*. Writings and paintings from the late Joseon dynasty, before 1910, describe it. It nearly disappeared in the 1900s. In 1983, South Korea named it an important cultural property. UNESCO listed it in 2011.

Some later books called taekkyeon the parent of taekwondo. Historians see a weaker link. Modern taekwondo grew mostly in the 1940s and 1950s. Taekkyeon and taekwondo are now separate arts with separate groups.

words.d: traditional Korean wrestling, held at village festivals; listed by UNESCO in 2018
an old Korean movement game; listed by UNESCO in 2011
a United Nations group that keeps lists of important world heritage, including living traditions

lessons.title: Pictures on Tomb Walls
lessons.mainIdea: Old wall paintings in Goguryeo tombs show wrestlers, but they do not prove that taekwondo is ancient.
reading: Goguryeo was a Korean kingdom. It lasted until 668 CE and ruled lands in today's North Korea and northeast China. Its rulers were buried in stone tombs. Inside, each wall holds a *mural*, a painting made right on the wall.

One tomb near the city of Ji'an, in China, is called Gakjeochong. The name means "tomb of the wrestlers." Its mural shows two men wrestling while an older man watches. Another tomb nearby, the Tomb of the Dancers, has hunters and dancers.

Some taekwondo books say these murals prove taekwondo is about 2,000 years old. That claim is a *legend*, a story many people repeat. Historians say the murals show old Korean wrestling and games. The art called taekwondo was built in the twentieth century.

words.d: a painting made directly on a wall
an old Korean kingdom that lasted until 668 CE and left painted tombs
a story many people repeat that records cannot prove

look.title: What Does the Wall Show?

look.prompt: What can this painting tell us for sure? What can it not tell us?

check.why: Historians say modern taekwondo was built in the twentieth century. The ancient claim is a legend.

lessons.title: The First Kwans
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1940s, Korean teachers who had studied in Japan opened training halls, called kwans, in Seoul.
reading: Japan ruled Korea as a colony from 1910 to 1945. Schools taught in Japanese. Some young Koreans went to Japan to study. A few learned karate at Japanese universities and dojos.

Some came home and opened halls in Seoul. A hall was called a *kwan*. Lee Won-kuk opened Chung Do Kwan in 1944. Hwang Kee opened Moo Duk Kwan in 1945, the year Korea was freed. By the mid-1940s, five main kwans taught in Seoul.

The halls used different names for their art. Some said *tang soo do*, a Korean way of saying the characters for "China hand way." Others said kong soo do, "empty hand way." The Korean War, from 1950 to 1953, closed many halls for a time.

words.d: a Korean word for a hall or school where an art is taught
an early Korean name for the art; it means China hand way
a land ruled by another country; Korea was a colony of Japan from 1910 to 1945

lessons.title: A Name Chosen in 1955
lessons.mainIdea: In 1955, a group led by army general Choi Hong-hi chose the name taekwondo.
reading: Choi Hong-hi was born in 1918 in the north of Korea. He studied in Japan and learned karate there. After 1945, he became an officer in South Korea's new army. He taught the art to soldiers.

In 1955, a group of teachers and leaders met to pick one name. They chose *taekwondo*, a name Choi put forward. Tae means "foot." Kwon means "fist." Do means "way." So taekwondo means "the way of the foot and fist."

The new name was Korean, not borrowed from Japanese. After years of *colonial rule*, many Koreans wanted a Korean name. Still, some kwans kept their old names for years. The name spread slowly, hall by hall.

words.d: a name chosen in 1955 that means the way of the foot and fist
when one country governs another land and its people; Japan ruled Korea this way from 1910 to 1945

look.prompt: Which name tells you where the art came from, and which tells you what the art uses?

choices: They had lived through years of Japanese colonial rule
check.why: After colonial rule from 1910 to 1945, many Koreans wanted a name that was Korean.

lessons.title: One Association for Many Halls
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1960s, the kwans joined one national association, which became the Korea Taekwondo Association in 1965.
reading: In the early 1960s, leaders of the kwans formed one national *association*. An association is a group that members join to work toward the same goals. It set shared ranks and rules for tests.

In 1965, the group took the name Korea Taekwondo Association. Most of its members still trained in the old kwans. Using one name everywhere helped the art look like one national sport, not a set of private halls.

The association sent teachers into schools, colleges and army units. South Korean troops in the Vietnam War, in the 1960s, carried taekwondo with them. Korean teachers also moved to the United States, Europe and other places to open schools.

words.d: a group that members join to work toward the same goals, such as shared ranks and rules
the national taekwondo group of South Korea, known by this name from 1965

look.prompt: How might one shared rank test help a student who moves to a new city?

check.why: The national group took the name Korea Taekwondo Association in 1965.

check.why: South Korean troops in Vietnam and teachers moving abroad spread taekwondo.

lessons.title: The Kukkiwon
lessons.mainIdea: The Kukkiwon, opened in Seoul in 1972, became taekwondo's world headquarters and gives black-belt certificates.
reading: In 1972, a large hall opened on a hill in Seoul. It is called the *Kukkiwon*. The name means roughly "hall of the national art." It holds events, trains teachers and runs rank tests.

The Kukkiwon gives out black-belt certificates. A *certificate* is an official paper that proves a rank. A student in Chicago or Cairo can hold a Kukkiwon certificate. That makes ranks match from country to country.

Children under 15 who pass a black-belt test get a *poom* rank. Poom is a junior black-belt rank. At age 15, a poom holder can change it to a dan, the adult black-belt rank. Kim Un-yong was an early leader of the Kukkiwon.

words.d: the world taekwondo headquarters in Seoul, opened in 1972; it gives black-belt certificates
an official paper that proves a rank or an achievement
a junior black-belt rank for taekwondo students under 15

lessons.title: Two World Federations
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo has two main world federations: the ITF, founded by Choi Hong-hi in 1966, and World Taekwondo, founded in 1973.
reading: In 1966, Choi Hong-hi founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation, or *ITF*, in Seoul. He later fell out with South Korea's government. In 1972, he moved the ITF's headquarters to Canada. The ITF later grew ties with North Korea.

In 1973, South Korea hosted the first world championships in Seoul. That same year, Kim Un-yong led the founding of a new *federation*, the World Taekwondo Federation. It changed its name to World Taekwondo, or WT, in 2017.

The two groups use different forms and different match rules. WT rules are the ones used at the Olympics. Choi died in 2002. After his death, the ITF split into several groups that each use the ITF name.

words.d: the International Taekwon-Do Federation, founded by Choi Hong-hi in 1966
a group of national bodies that agree on one set of rules
the world federation founded in 1973 whose rules are used at the Olympics

lessons.title: Not Just Korean Karate
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo began with ties to karate, but Korean leaders gave it its own forms, words and scoring rules.
reading: Early kwan founders had learned karate, so their first routines came from karate. Later, Korean groups wrote new routines of their own. In taekwondo these set routines are called *poomsae*. Their names come from Korean ideas and history.

Commands and counting in a taekwondo room are in Korean. The uniform is called a *dobok*. World Taekwondo rules give more points for kicks than for punches. So taekwondo matches came to look very different from karate matches.

In 2018, South Korea's lawmakers named taekwondo the country's national martial art. Calling it "Korean karate" hides these changes. Historians describe taekwondo as a new Korean art with karate among its roots.

words.d: the Korean word for set routines in taekwondo
the Korean word for the taekwondo uniform

lessons.title: From Show to Medals
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo was a demonstration sport in 1988 and 1992 and became a full Olympic medal sport at Sydney 2000.
reading: Seoul hosted the Summer Olympics in 1988. Taekwondo appeared there as a *demonstration sport*. That means athletes competed, but the medals did not count in the official Olympic totals. It was a demonstration sport again at Barcelona in 1992.

In 1994, the IOC voted to add taekwondo to the program for Sydney 2000. At Sydney, athletes competed in eight groups by body weight, four for men and four for women. Players in each *weight class* weigh about the same, which keeps matches fair.

Steven López of Texas won a gold medal for the United States at Sydney. Chen Zhong won gold for China. Lauren Burns won gold for Australia, the host country. Taekwondo has been part of every Summer Olympics since then.

words.d: a sport shown at the Olympics whose medals do not count in official totals
a group of athletes who weigh about the same and compete against each other

lessons.title: New Tools, New Athletes
lessons.mainIdea: Electronic scoring, the Paralympics and athletes from new countries changed Olympic taekwondo in the 2000s.
reading: For years, judges pressed buttons to score taekwondo points. Arguments about scores were common. At the London 2012 Olympics, athletes wore *electronic scoring* vests with sensors. The vests help count points in a fairer, clearer way.

Para taekwondo joined the *Paralympics* at the Tokyo 2020 Games, held in 2021. The Paralympics are the Games for athletes with disabilities. They come right after the Olympics in the same host city. Para taekwondo athletes compete in groups based on their disability and weight.

Taekwondo has brought Olympic medals to countries that had few before. At the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Olympics, Kimia Alizadeh won bronze in taekwondo. She became the first Iranian woman to win an Olympic medal. World Taekwondo now has more than 200 member countries.

words.d: a system of sensors that helps count points, used in Olympic taekwondo since London 2012
the Games for athletes with disabilities, held after the Olympics in the same city
